exercises.solution:
Full statement. A pseudorandom function ensemble is a collection { f_s : {0,1}^{|s|} -> {0,1}^{|s|} }_{s in {0,1}^*} satisfying:

1. (Efficient evaluation) There exists an efficient deterministic algorithm A such that for every seed s and every x in {0,1}^{|s|}, A(s, x) = f_s(x). 'Efficient' here means running in time polynomial in |s| (hence also in |x| = |s|).

2. (Pseudorandomness) For every probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine M, for every positive polynomial p(.), there exists an integer k_0 such that for all k >= k_0,
   |Pr_{s<-U_k, r}[ M^{f_s}(1^k) = 1 ] - Pr_{F, r}[ M^{F}(1^k) = 1 ]| < 1/p(k),
   where U_k is uniform on {0,1}^k, F is a uniformly random function {0,1}^k -> {0,1}^k, and r denotes M's internal coin tosses.

Ingredient-by-ingredient annotation:

(i) The ensemble. The collection is indexed by all seeds s in {0,1}^*, and for a k-bit seed the member is a function on k-bit strings. Without the index-by-seed structure there is nothing to share in applications and no 'random' choice to speak of: the definition's randomness enters precisely by drawing s uniformly. (An unkeyed single function could only be compared against itself.)

(ii) Efficient evaluation. A(s, x) = f_s(x) in polynomial time is what makes the object usable at all: applications must compute values on demand, and the oracle machine's queries must be answerable. If evaluation were not efficient, the honest parties could not use f_s, and there would be no algorithm witnessing that the pseudorandom object is 'constructible'. Note the algorithm is deterministic — f_s must be a function, not a fresh sample.

(iii) The oracle machine M. M is the distinguisher, upgraded to an oracle machine because the object under test is a function. Its input 1^k (k in unary) makes its runtime, its number of queries, and the query/answer length all polynomial in the seed length k. The probabilities range over M's coins as well as the oracle: M may be randomized, and its random choices are part of the test. Without the 1^k input, 'polynomial time' would have no length parameter tied to the security parameter.

(iv) The reference object F_k. A uniformly random function from {0,1}^k to {0,1}^k plays the role that U_{ell(k)} played for PRGs: it is the 'truly random' benchmark. It is not something an efficient machine can hold or sample explicitly — it is a distribution used only in the definition (and in proofs, as the endpoint of hybrid arguments). If the benchmark were, say, a single fixed function, the notion would be meaningless, since any fixed function has an obvious distinguisher.

(v) The quantifier order. 'For every PPT M, for every polynomial p, for all sufficiently large k' says: the gap is negligible as a function of k; each machine's gap may shrink at its own rate, and the inequality must hold eventually, for all large k. The order cannot be permuted: 'there exists p such that for all M' would let the bound depend on nothing and would be trivially satisfiable or impossible; 'for all k' without 'sufficiently large' would let finitely many small k (where a machine could simply enumerate functions) kill the definition; and p must come after M because different machines may be distinguishable with different gaps — the requirement is only that every machine's gap is eventually below every polynomial reciprocal. Negation discipline confirms this reading: the family is NOT a PRF iff some PPT M and some polynomial p have gap >= 1/p(k) infinitely often, which is exactly the formal meaning of 'distinguishable with non-negligible advantage'.

(i) G maps {0,1}^k to {0,1}^{2k^2} (length m(k)·k with m(k) = 2k), so the stretch is ell(k) = 2k^2 > k, and ell is polynomial-time computable. G is efficiently computable: by condition (1) of Definition 2.17 each value f_s(x_i) is obtained in polynomial time by the evaluation algorithm, and there are m(k) = poly(k) of them, so the whole concatenation takes polynomial time in k.

(ii) Let D be any PPT distinguisher and let gap(k) = |Pr[D(G(U_k)) = 1] - Pr[D(U_{2k^2}) = 1]|. We build a PPT oracle machine M: on input 1^k, M queries its oracle at x_1, ..., x_{m(k)}; let a_i be the i-th answer; set z = a_1 ... a_{m(k)} (length m(k)·k = 2k^2); output D(z).

Claim: Pr[M^{f_{U_k}}(1^k) = 1] = Pr[D(G(U_k)) = 1], because when the oracle is f_s for s <- U_k, the answers are exactly f_s(x_1), ..., f_s(x_{m(k)}), whose concatenation is G(s).

Claim: Pr[M^{F_k}(1^k) = 1] = Pr[D(U_{2k^2}) = 1]. Indeed, when the oracle is a uniformly random function F_k, the answers at the pairwise distinct points x_1, ..., x_{m(k)} are independent random variables, each uniform on {0,1}^k: a random function's values are independent across its domain, and distinct arguments have independent values. Hence z is uniform on {0,1}^{m(k)·k}, i.e., distributed as U_{2k^2}.

Therefore |Pr[M^{f_{U_k}}(1^k)=1] - Pr[M^{F_k}(1^k)=1]| = gap(k). Since M is a PPT oracle machine asking m(k) = 2k = poly(k) queries, the pseudorandomness condition of Definition 2.17 applies: for every polynomial p and all sufficiently large k, gap(k) < 1/p(k). So gap is negligible, and since D was arbitrary, G is a pseudorandom generator.

(iii) Why fixed queries are fine: Definition 2.17 requires indistinguishability against every probabilistic polynomial-time oracle machine. The machine M we constructed is non-adaptive — its query list x_1, ..., x_m is hard-wired before any answer arrives — and non-adaptive machines are a subset of adaptive ones. Since the definition's guarantee covers all machines in the larger (adaptive) class, it certainly covers M. No adaptivity was needed for this direction; the asymmetry is that the converse direction (GGM, Theorem 2.18) must produce functions that fool even adaptive machines, which is why its hybrid proof is more delicate.

Where distinctness is used: in the second claim. A truly random function is consistent — querying the same point twice returns the same value — and independent at distinct points. The ideal string z is uniform precisely because the x_i are pairwise distinct, so no block of z is forced to equal another. If two inputs coincided (say x_1 = x_2), then under F_k the first two blocks of z would be equal with probability 1, while under G(U_k) they would also be equal (both are f_s at the same point) — but the 'uniform' benchmark would have independent blocks, so comparing against U would be the wrong benchmark and the claimed equality in the second claim would fail. Pairwise distinctness is what makes the random-function answers behave like independent uniform samples.

(a) A non-adaptive oracle machine chooses its entire query list q_1, ..., q_t up front, then reads the answers a_1, ..., a_t. An adaptive machine chooses each query as a function of everything seen so far: q_{i+1} may depend on (q_1, a_1, ..., q_i, a_i) and on its own coin tosses. Adaptive strategies are strictly more expressive. Concrete adaptive-only test: probing the graph of the function — query x, receive y, then query y and check whether the answer equals some predicted value (e.g., whether f(y) = x). The second query cannot be chosen until the first answer arrives, because its content is the first answer itself.

(b) A distinguisher is by definition a binary decision: it outputs 1 on the distribution it 'thinks' it saw (up to the usual convention of which side accepts). Suppose a machine M' outputs a richer verdict v (a string, or a real number). Any event we care about — 'M' accepts', 'v > 0.7', 'v matches a guess' — is a (possibly randomized) predicate of M's transcript plus coins. Build M that runs M' internally, computing the full transcript, then outputs 1 exactly when that predicate holds. M is still a PPT oracle machine (it does everything M' did, plus one comparison) and its acceptance probability is exactly the probability of the event under each experiment. Since every test is an event, single-bit output captures all tests; allowing longer outputs would only add notation, not power. This is the same reason PRG definitions use 1-bit distinguishers.

(c) Determinism of the oracle means repeated queries return the same answer, so an adaptive machine cannot 'learn more' by re-asking — but that is not where adaptivity's power lies. Its power is in targeting: the machine chooses where to look next based on what it found, and can follow structure (chains, cycles, relations) that a fixed list would have to guess blindly. Concretely, let family A consist of all involutions with no fixed points? (use any involution: f(f(x)) = x for all x) and family B the single truly random function. Adaptive machine: query x_0, get y; query y, get z; accept iff z = x_0. Under an involution this always accepts; under a random function, y is uniform and independent of x_0, so z = f(y) is uniform and equals x_0 with probability exactly 2^{-k} — the machine separates the families with 2 queries and advantage 1 - 2^{-k}. A non-adaptive machine with q = poly(k) queries sees, in both worlds, q answers at distinct points: under an involution the answers are q distinct points; under a random function the answers are distinct except with probability about q^2/2^{k+1}, which is negligible. The two transcripts are statistically indistinguishable (both look like q distinct uniform strings), so no non-adaptive machine with polynomially many queries separates them. This shows adaptivity is a genuine strengthening — and why Definition 2.17, which must be the strongest reasonable formulation, quantifies over adaptive machines.
